title: Sermones Ad Populum. Classis II. De Tempore
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa013c.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: et nutritos servos pervisibilem formam servi, perficit liberos ad videndam formam Dei. Filii enim Dei 2sumus9 et nondum appadicis sermone Hi. Sed verius sunt Ambrosiani cujusdam sermonis de Natali Domini, teste Cassiano in libro septimo de Incarnatione. ruit quid erimus. Et scimus quoniam cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est (1 Joan. III, 2). Nam qui sunt illi sapientiæ scientiaqne thesauri, quæ illæ divitiæ divinæ, nisi quia sufficiunt nobis Ą Et quæ illa multitudo dulcedinis, nisi quia satiat nos?
passages.english: and, having nourished [us as] servants through the visible form of a servant, he makes [us] free to see the form of God. For we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. And we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). For what are those treasures of wisdom and knowledge, what are those divine riches, except that they suffice for us? And what is that abundance of sweetness, except that it satisfies us?
passages.notes: The source text has an editorial footnote spliced into the middle of the biblical quotation: "appadicis sermone Hi. Sed verius sunt Ambrosiani cujusdam sermonis de Natali Domini, teste Cassiano in libro septimo de Incarnatione. ruit". It means roughly "... in the appendix sermon. But they rather belong to a certain sermon of Ambrose on the Lord's Nativity, as Cassian attests in the seventh book On the Incarnation". It has been omitted, and the quotation reconstructed as "nondum apparuit quid erimus". The note presumably concerns the attribution of these words to Ambrose. "2sumus9" is read as "sumus". The stray "Ą" is taken as a question mark.

passages.original: tamen habet corpus istud speciem suam , dispositionem membrorum, distinctionem sensuum, erectam staturam, et cætera quae bene considerantes stupent. Verumtamen illud omnino incorruptibile, omnino immortale, omnino ad movendum agile et facile erit. Sed ait Porphyrius : Sine causa mihi laudas corpus; qualecumque sit corpus, si vult esse beata anima , corpus est omne fugiendum. Hoc dicunt philosophi: sed errant, sed delirant. Cito probo : nolo diutius disputare ;
passages.english: yet this body has its own beauty: the arrangement of its limbs, the distinctness of its senses, its upright stature, and the other things at which those who consider them well are amazed. But that [body] will be wholly incorruptible, wholly immortal, wholly nimble and easy in movement. But Porphyry says: 'You praise the body to me for no reason; whatever the body is like, if the soul wishes to be happy, every body must be fled.' This is what the philosophers say: but they are wrong, they are raving. I prove it quickly; I do not want to argue at length;
